messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 33
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Physical Therapist
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 38

# Marcus

Marcus sits in the clinic waiting room with his shoulders drawn up toward his ears, his knee bouncing in a steady rhythm that he doesn't seem aware of. At thirty-three, he looks older—there's a tightness around his eyes that suggests he hasn't slept well in months. He's a physical therapist at a busy outpatient clinic, a profession he chose because he's always been drawn to helping people move through pain. His wife, Priya, had to drive him to this appointment because he still doesn't feel safe behind the wheel.

Fourteen months ago, Marcus was driving home from work on a familiar highway when a delivery truck crossed the median without warning. The collision was violent and sudden. He remembers the sound of metal crumpling, the sensation of the car spinning, and then darkness. He woke in the hospital with a fractured pelvis, three broken ribs, and injuries that took months to heal physically. But the physical wounds have largely mended. The other injuries remain.

Now, when Marcus drives—on the rare occasions he attempts it—his hands grip the steering wheel so tightly they go numb. His heart races at unpredictable moments. He finds himself scanning the road obsessively, watching the movements of other vehicles with an intensity that exhausts him. Last month, a car changed lanes suddenly in front of him, and Marcus pulled over, trembling, unable to continue. Priya has become the driver in their household, and Marcus carries a quiet shame about this that he doesn't voice but that she can feel.

The accident has infiltrated his professional life in unexpected ways. At work, Marcus helps patients regain mobility and strength. He's good at his job—patient, knowledgeable, genuinely invested in people's recovery. But lately, he's been having trouble concentrating during treatment sessions. His mind drifts. Sometimes, while working with a patient, he'll suddenly become hyperaware of the room's exits, or he'll notice his own breathing has become shallow and rapid. Last week, a patient moved too quickly during an exercise, and Marcus flinched so visibly that the patient asked if he was okay. He made an excuse about a muscle cramp.

Sleep has become a minefield. Marcus lies awake beside Priya, his mind replaying the accident in fragmented, distorted ways. Sometimes he dreams of it happening again, but with different, worse outcomes. He wakes gasping, his shirt soaked with sweat, and has to remind himself—out loud, sometimes—that he's home, that he's safe. Priya has learned not to touch him when he wakes this way; his startle response is too intense. He feels her disappointment in the careful distance she maintains now.

The worst part, Marcus says, is the unpredictability. He can go two days feeling almost normal, then something small will trigger him—a sound like screeching tires, the smell of gasoline, even certain songs that were playing in the hospital—and he's right back there. His body reacts before his mind can catch up. His chest tightens. His palms sweat. The world feels dangerous in a way it didn't before.

He's withdrawn from friends, turned down a promotion that would have required more driving, and started second-guessing his ability to continue in physical therapy. Some days, he wonders if he'll ever feel like himself again, or if this hypervigilant, fragile version of Marcus is permanent now. Priya says he will heal, but Marcus isn't sure she really believes it anymore. He isn't sure he does either.
